newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine makes global compromise on planes and cars.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine makes global compromise on planes and cars.

text.p: Ukraine, desperate for foreign investment to boost its troubled economy, has tried to please West and East by splitting two tenders on planes and cars between competing U.S., European and Asian giants.
Ukraine announced on Monday it was awarding a contract fought out by U.S. giant Boeing Co and Europe's Airbus Industrie to both of them.
Analysts said Kiev was also seizing a chance to fend off criticism that its investment climate was being damaged by corrupt government officials and cancelled agreements.
State-owned Air Ukraine will buy two Boeing 767-200ER airliners for its transatlantic routes and three Airbus A320-200s for medium-range flights in a start to replacing its ageing Soviet fleet.

In a seperate development Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko announced on Tuesday that General Motors and South Korea's Daewoo Group would form a joint venture to produce cars at the AvtoZAZ car plant in the city of Zaporizhya.

"These are compromise decisions," said Svitlana Dubrovska, a leading analyst at the Den daily. "Also Ukraine -- especially historically -- is afraid of a diktat from one source. That's why it wants to keep some balance even among investors."
The decision on planes had been postponed several times in recent months. Ukrainian media had said Airbus was favoured last year, but Boeing improved its chances of winning the order in 1997.

An investment tender to find a strategic investor for AvtoZAZ, Ukraine's only car plant, was launched in 1996 but officially announced only earlier this year. Both Daewoo and GM had been considered the only serious competitors.
"The government was afraid to push U.S. companies out of the Ukrainian market especially after the scandal with Motorola and some other U.S. investors," Dubrovska said.
She was referring to an announcement in March that the U.S. giant was pulling out of a mobile phones deal potentially worth half a billion dollars due to ever-changing conditions.
Several Western newspapers like The New York Times have recently published articles telling of instability, high-level corruption and a risky investment climate.

"The loss of some powerful competitors could inspire another wave of suspicions," one analyst said, adding that the four successful foreign companies had been fighting hard to win. "All of them have powerful lobbies here but the rivalries were going on under the carpet."

Lazarenko stressed that the decision on the plane purchases had not been politically motivated, adding: "There was a tender and it is better to have Boeings flying transatlantic routes and Airbuses flying to Europe".

Some experts said Ukraine might benefit from having various foreign strategic partners. "From a technical point of view it is not a problem when a carrier uses different types of planes. Spanish Iberia flies with 14 types no problem," Vadym Sorokin, vice-president of Ukraine International Airlines told Reuters.
"The competition between two partners would help reduce the price of goods and services and avoid dominance," he added.

Lazarenko said recently that both Boeing and Airbus had cut their prices by $10 million each per plane. He also said 1997 would herald foreign investments of between $800 million and $1.2 billion. Ukraine has attracted only $1.4 billion since 1991.
